note.explanation: Racing cars and balancing toys are designed using ideas about stability. A low centre of mass and a wide base help a car resist toppling. In a balancing toy, the centre of gravity is below the pivot, so disturbing the toy raises its centre of gravity; it returns to its stable position by lowering it. In circular motion, the velocity points along the tangent, while the force needed to keep the body moving in a circle acts perpendicular to the velocity.
examples: A racing car is made more stable by keeping its centre of mass low and its wheels outside the main body, which increases its base area.
A balancing toy returns to its original position after it is disturbed because it lowers its centre of gravity.
note.checkAnswer: A low centre of mass and a wide base area.
note.simple: A low, wide object is harder to tip over. A balancing toy returns to its resting position by lowering its centre of gravity. In circular motion, the force points inward and the velocity points along the circle’s tangent.
note.checkQuestion: What two design features improve the stability of a racing car?
note.title: Stability and motion in a circle
steps: Keep the centre of mass as low as possible.
Increase the base area, for example by keeping the wheels outside the main body.
For a balancing toy, identify the pivot and check that its centre of gravity is below it.
For circular motion, draw the velocity along the tangent and the force towards the centre; these directions are perpendicular.
note.answer: A racing car is made more stable by keeping its centre of mass low and increasing its base area. A balancing toy returns to its stable position by lowering its centre of gravity. A body moving in a circle has velocity along the tangent and needs a force perpendicular to its velocity to keep moving in the circle.

written.text: A car travels at the same speed around two curves with different radii. For which radius the car experiences more centripetal force? Prove your answer.
written.finalAnswer: The car experiences more centripetal force on the curve with the smaller radius, because F = mv²/r.

rubric.why: The comparison requires recognising that the car's mass and speed are unchanged.
rubric.description: Identify that the mass and speed are the same on both curves.
rubric.how: State that the car travels at the same speed and compare the same car on both curves.

rubric.why: The centripetal-force relationship shows how force depends on radius.
rubric.description: Write the centripetal-force relation.
rubric.how: Use F = mv²/r.

rubric.why: At fixed mass and speed, force increases as radius decreases.
rubric.description: Compare the forces for the two radii.
rubric.how: Explain that the smaller radius gives the greater force.

rubric.why: The conclusion directly answers which curve requires more force.
rubric.description: Give the correct final conclusion.
rubric.how: State that the car experiences more centripetal force on the curve with the smaller radius.

modelAnswer: Centripetal force is given by F = mv²/r.
The mass and speed of the car are the same for both curves.
Therefore, F is inversely proportional to r.
So the car experiences more centripetal force on the curve with the smaller radius.

written.text: Why an accelerated body cannot be considered in equilibrium?
written.finalAnswer: An accelerated body cannot be in equilibrium because its acceleration shows that a resultant force acts on it; in equilibrium, the resultant force is zero.

rubric.why: Acceleration indicates that the body's motion is changing.
rubric.description: Connect acceleration with a resultant force.
rubric.how: State that an accelerated body has a resultant force acting on it.

rubric.why: Equilibrium requires no resultant force.
rubric.description: State the force condition for equilibrium.
rubric.how: Write that the resultant force in equilibrium is zero.

rubric.why: This links the given situation to the definition of equilibrium.
rubric.description: Apply the equilibrium condition to an accelerated body.
rubric.how: Explain that acceleration and zero resultant force cannot both describe the body.

rubric.why: The final statement must answer the question clearly.
rubric.description: State the conclusion.
rubric.how: Conclude that an accelerated body cannot be considered in equilibrium.

modelAnswer: An accelerated body has a resultant force acting on it.
In equilibrium, the resultant force on a body is zero.
Therefore, an accelerated body cannot be considered in equilibrium.

written.text: Two boxes of the same weight but different heights are lying on the floor of a truck. If the truck makes a sudden stop, which box is more likely to tumble over? Why?
written.finalAnswer: The taller box is more likely to tumble over because its centre of gravity is higher.

written.text: Discuss the concepts of stability and centre of gravity in relation to objects toppling over. Provide an example where an object’s centre of gravity affects its stability, and explain how altering its base of support can influence stability.
written.finalAnswer: An object is more stable when its centre of gravity is low and its base of support is wide. For example, a racing car is made more stable by keeping its centre of mass low and its wheels outside its main body, increasing its base area.

written.text: A ripe mango does not normally fall from the tree. But when the branch of the tree is shaken, the mango falls down easily. Can you tell the reason?
written.finalAnswer: When the branch is shaken, it moves suddenly but the mango tends to remain in its state of rest due to inertia. The stalk may break, and the mango falls.

The stalk may break because of this relative motion.

written.text: How the stability of an object can be improved? Give a few examples to support your answer.
written.finalAnswer: The stability of an object can be improved by lowering its centre of mass and increasing its base area. For example, racing cars have a low centre of mass and wheels outside their main bodies; balancing toys return to their stable position by lowering their centre of gravity.

written.text: How can you prove that the centripetal force always acts perpendicular to velocity?
written.finalAnswer: The velocity of a body moving in a circle is along the tangent. If the force had a component along the velocity, it would change the magnitude of velocity. For constant speed, that component must be zero, so the force is perpendicular to velocity.

rubric.why: The tangent gives the direction of velocity in circular motion.
rubric.description: State the direction of velocity.
rubric.how: Write that velocity at any point is along the tangent to the circle.

rubric.why: A force component along velocity would affect the speed.
rubric.description: Consider a possible force component along velocity.
rubric.how: State that a component of force along velocity would change its magnitude.

rubric.why: For uniform speed, the component that changes speed must vanish.
rubric.description: Use the constant-speed condition.
rubric.how: Explain that the component along velocity is zero; the section expresses this as F cos 90° = 0.

rubric.why: The conclusion directly answers the question.
rubric.description: State the perpendicular relationship.
rubric.how: Conclude that the centripetal force is perpendicular to velocity.

modelAnswer: The velocity at any point on a circular path is directed along the tangent.
If the force were not perpendicular to velocity, it would have a component in the direction of velocity.
This component would change the magnitude of velocity.
As the body moves with constant speed, this component is zero: F cos 90° = 0.
Therefore, the centripetal force acts perpendicular to velocity.

examTips: This section can be tested through a short-answer question asking for the two principles used to improve stability: keep the centre of mass low and increase the base area.

A constructed-response question may ask why an object is more likely to topple. Identify the centre of gravity and base of support, then link a high centre of gravity or narrow base to reduced stability.
For circular motion, questions may ask for the direction of velocity and force. State that velocity is along the tangent and the required force is perpendicular to it.
To earn explanation marks, connect the fact to its effect: a force component along velocity changes the speed, while a perpendicular force changes the direction of velocity.

explain.title: How racing cars are made stable
explain.body: Racing cars move fast and take sharp turns, so they may topple. Their centre of mass is kept as low as possible. Their base area is increased by keeping the wheels outside the main body.

explain.title: Why balancing toys return
explain.body: In these toys, the centre of gravity remains below the pivot in the stable position. When disturbed, the centre of gravity rises. The toy returns to its original stable position by lowering its centre of gravity.

explain.title: Rotational motion and translational motion
explain.body: The section pairs velocity with angular velocity, acceleration with angular acceleration, force with torque, and momentum with angular momentum. Torque plays the role in rotational motion that force plays in translational motion.

explain.title: Velocity and force in circular motion
explain.body: The velocity of a body moving in a circle points along the tangent at each point. The direction of the tangent changes around the circle, so the velocity changes direction. A force perpendicular to velocity is needed to keep the body moving at constant speed in a circle.

mistakes: Do not say that a racing car is made more stable by raising its centre of mass; the section says it is kept as low as possible.
Do not confuse the tangent direction of velocity with the inward direction of the force in circular motion.
Do not say that a force along the velocity keeps the speed constant; a component along velocity changes the magnitude of velocity.
Do not forget the second racing-car design feature: increasing the base area by keeping the wheels outside the main body.
